bank.keyText: It stays the same, because the outside is also 300 mOsm

answer.text: It stays the same, because the outside is also 300 mOsm
answer.line: 0.15 M NaCl is 300 mOsm, the same as the inside, so water has no net reason to move.

steps: Count particles, not formula units. NaCl splits into Na+ and Cl-, so 0.15 M becomes 0.15 x 2 = 0.30 osmol per liter.
0.30 osmol per liter is 300 mOsm. The inside is 300 mOsm too.
Same on both sides is isotonic. Water still crosses, but equally both ways. No net flow, no change in volume.

choices.text: It stays the same, because the outside is also 300 mOsm
choices.note: 0.15 M x 2 particles = 300 mOsm. A match for the inside.

choices.text: It swells, because sodium enters and water follows it in
choices.note: Swelling is what a solute that crosses, like urea, would cause. Na+ gets pumped back out, so it acts as if it stays outside, and 300 against 300 moves no water.

choices.text: It shrinks, because 300 mOsm of NaCl outdraws the cytoplasm
choices.note: The 300 is right. But 300 equals 300, and water only moves toward a difference.

choices.text: It swells, because 150 mOsm outside is well below the 300 mOsm inside
choices.note: 150 is the NaCl before it splits. Each unit gives two ions, so the outside is 300.

choices.text: It shrinks, because 0.15 M NaCl comes to 600 mOsm
choices.note: NaCl gives two particles, not four. 0.15 x 2 = 0.30 osmol per liter, which is 300 mOsm.

lockIt: Osmolarity is molarity times particles. Water moves only when the two sides differ.
hook: Count the ions: NaCl gives 2, CaCl2 gives 3, glucose gives 1.

playWith.label: Tonicity simulator: set the outside to match the inside and watch the red cells hold their shape

visual.alt: Top: a tally turning 0.15 M NaCl into 0.15 M Na+ plus 0.15 M Cl-, 300 mOsm outside, next to 300 mOsm inside, an even balance. Bottom: a light microscope view of red blood cells in a matched solution, normal biconcave discs, with no net water flow.
visual.caption: Count ions, then compare. Equal on both sides, so the cells keep their normal disc shape.
